bug_description.original: Heap-buffer-overflow (out-of-bounds read) in PackMachBase::canUnpack (p_mach.cpp) via get_ne32/get_le32 (bele.h). While iterating Mach-O load commands (including fat/32-bit paths), a malformed or too-short command can cause a 4-byte read past the allocated buffer, leading to crashes and possible disclosure of heap memory.
bug_description.normalized: The staged fat Mach-O testcase is admitted by `PackMachFat::canUnpack()`, which eventually selects the second i386 slice at offset `0x8000`. That slice's inner Mach header advertises `filetype = MH_DYLIB`, so the first `PackMachI386::canUnpack()` attempt returns false on the filetype check and `PackMachFat::canUnpack()` falls back to `PackDylibI386::canUnpack()` on the same bounded slice. In the shared `PackMachBase::canUnpack()` implementation, the fallback parser accepts `ncmds = 219` and `sizeofcmds = 3028`, allocates a 3028-byte `rawmseg` buffer, and copies exactly that many load-command bytes into it. The 44 complete load commands present in the slice have `cmdsize` values that sum exactly to 3028, so after the 44th command the loop state becomes `headway == 0` and `ptr == rawmseg + sizeofcmds` while `j < ncmds` still holds. Vulnerable code then starts the next iteration and reads `ptr->cmdsize` before checking that a full `Mach_command` remains, producing the saved 4-byte heap-buffer-overflow read in `get_ne32`.

source.description: First project-code materialization point on the witnessed path. UPX copies the attacker-controlled outer fat header and its architecture table into `fat_head`, creating the slice metadata that later selects the crashing i386 Mach-O parser.
source.value_from: The staged `poc` begins with the big-endian bytes `ca fe ba be 00 00 00 02`, then two fat-arch entries. The second entry encodes `cputype = 0x7`, `offset = 0x8000`, and `size = 0x66d0`, which are the exact values later used to expose the crashing i386 slice.

sink.description: AddressSanitizer-observed sink. On the failing fallback iteration `ptr` already equals `rawmseg + sizeofcmds`, so converting `ptr->cmdsize` performs a 4-byte load from the first byte past the 3028-byte heap buffer and trips the saved heap-buffer-overflow in `get_ne32`.

root_cause.code: for (unsigned j= 0; j < ncmds; ptr = (Mach_command const *)(ptr->cmdsize + (char const *)ptr), ++j) {
root_cause.description: Root cause fixed by commit `a49d023bd04c585ac4c342c90d214c9aef2c8b08`. The loop is re-entered solely while `j < ncmds`; vulnerable code has no `headway < (int)sizeof(Mach_command)` check before the loop body dereferences `ptr`, so a file can advertise more commands than there are complete `Mach_command` prefixes in the `sizeofcmds` buffer.

tainted_value_origin.description: This inner Mach-header read in the fallback dylib parser materializes the vulnerability-driving header fields from the selected i386 slice. In the staged testcase those fields become `ncmds = 219` and `sizeofcmds = 3028`, the pair that later leaves the loop asking for another command after the copied buffer is already exhausted.

parser_admitted.description: Sample-specific fat-Mach admission gate. The staged file starts with `FAT_MAGIC`, `nfat = 2`, and two aligned in-bounds arch entries, so `check_fat_head()` returns 2 and this rejection branch is not taken.

coarse_trace.summary: UPX reads and validates the outer fat Mach-O container, then reaches the second architecture entry at offset `0x8000`; the first `PackMachI386::canUnpack()` attempt rejects the slice's `MH_DYLIB` filetype and `PackMachFat::canUnpack()` falls back to `PackDylibI386`.
The fallback dylib parser accepts the selected i386 Mach header with `ncmds = 219` and `sizeofcmds = 3028`, so UPX allocates a 3028-byte heap buffer and copies the load-command area into `rawmseg`.
During load-command iteration, the 44 complete commands present in `rawmseg` consume all 3028 bytes, leaving `headway == 0` and `ptr == rawmseg + sizeofcmds` even though `j < ncmds` still holds.

Because the loop lacks a pre-read `headway >= sizeof(Mach_command)` guard, the next iteration dereferences `ptr->cmdsize` from one past the heap buffer end and AddressSanitizer reports the out-of-bounds read.

fine_trace.note: UPX copies the testcase's outer fat header and the first five `fat_arch` slots into `fat_head`. For this sample the copied bytes contain `FAT_MAGIC`, `nfat = 2`, and a second arch entry whose `cputype`, `offset`, and `size` later steer execution into the crashing i386 slice.

`check_fat_head()` validates the copied container metadata: `fat_head.fat.magic == FAT_MAGIC`, `nfat == 2`, each arch alignment is within 12..24, and both `offset + size` ranges stay inside the 59088-byte file. The outer parser therefore keeps processing this sample instead of returning 0 or throwing on malformed fat-arch metadata.

When the loop reaches `j == 1`, the validated second `fat_arch` entry exposes the i386 slice as a 26320-byte subfile at offset `0x8000`. The subsequent `switch (arch[j].cputype)` takes the `CPU_TYPE_I386` case on exactly that bounded slice.

The first `PackMachI386::canUnpack()` attempt reads the selected slice's Mach header. In the staged testcase the copied header is little-endian `0xfeedface` with `cputype = 0x7`, `filetype = 0x6`, `ncmds = 219`, and `sizeofcmds = 3028`.

The executable parser rejects this slice before any command-buffer allocation. `PackMachI386` was constructed with `my_filetype = MH_EXECUTE`, but the sample header says `mhdri.filetype == MH_DYLIB`, so the guard returns false and the crashing instance must come from the fallback path instead.

The true `!packer.canUnpack()` branch creates the i386 dylib fallback on the same bounded slice. `PackDylibI386` resets `my_filetype` to `MH_DYLIB` in its constructor at line 240, and line 2613 immediately invokes this fallback parser; the saved AddressSanitizer caller frame points at that fallback call site.

The fallback `PackDylibI386::canUnpack()` rereads the same inner Mach header from the slice start. With `my_filetype` now set to `MH_DYLIB`, the copied header is admissible for the vulnerable shared parser.

fine_trace.code:
unsigned const ncmds = mhdri.ncmds;
int headway = (int)mhdri.sizeofcmds;
fine_trace.note: UPX derives the loop bounds from the attacker-controlled header and accepts them. Here `ncmds` becomes 219 and `headway` becomes 3028, which passes the early header checks because `MAX_N_CMDS` is 256, the selected slice `file_size` is 26320 after `set_extent`, and 3028 is far larger than the minimum header area required for 3 Mach commands.

The accepted `sizeofcmds` value directly determines the heap allocation size for the command buffer. AddressSanitizer's allocation stack for the crashing region points back to this statement, which requests exactly 3028 bytes.

UPX fills the new heap buffer with exactly 3028 bytes of load-command data from the selected i386 slice. Every later `ptr->cmd` and `ptr->cmdsize` read in this loop is expected to stay within this copied `rawmseg` region.

Across the first 44 accepted load commands, each decoded `cmdsize` is subtracted from `headway`. In this sample the last complete command starts at offset 3012 and has `cmdsize = 16`, so after `j == 43` this subtraction alone consumes the final 16 bytes of the 3028-byte command buffer and leaves `headway == 0`.

After that last in-bounds command, the `for` update expression uses the same `cmdsize = 16` to advance `ptr` from the last command start at `rawmseg + 3012` to `rawmseg + 3028`, and increments `j` from 43 to 44. The next iteration therefore begins with `ptr` already one Mach-command header past the copied heap buffer.

Root-cause control decision. The loop re-enters because `j == 44` still satisfies `j < ncmds` (`219`), and vulnerable code has no `headway < (int)sizeof(Mach_command)` guard before the body dereferences `ptr`, even though step 11 already established `headway == 0`.

Sink. On fallback iteration 44, `ptr` still equals `rawmseg + 3028`, so `ptr->cmdsize` reads the next 4-byte little-endian word from the first byte past the heap buffer. The saved AddressSanitizer trace attributes the fault to `get_ne32()` via `get_le32()` and `LE32::operator unsigned()` at this statement in `PackMachBase<...MachClass_32...>::canUnpack()`.

format.name: fat Mach-O with an i386 slice
format.contract: The witness begins with big-endian `FAT_MAGIC` and `nfat_arch = 2`. The second fat-arch entry is `CPU_TYPE_I386` with `offset = 0x8000` and `size = 0x66d0`. At that offset the little-endian Mach header is `MH_MAGIC`, `cputype = 0x7`, `filetype = 0x6` (`MH_DYLIB`), `ncmds = 219`, and `sizeofcmds = 3028`, so the first `PackMachI386::canUnpack()` attempt returns false on `my_filetype != mhdri.filetype` and `PackMachFat::canUnpack()` falls back to `PackDylibI386::canUnpack()`. The 3028-byte load-command region contains only 44 complete commands whose `cmdsize` values sum exactly to 3028, so the loop reaches `j = 44` with `headway == 0` and `ptr == rawmseg + sizeofcmds` while `j < ncmds` still holds.
